entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works, established in 1886 in Berne, Switzerland, represents a pivotal moment in the global evolution of copyright law. This treaty, initiated by notable figures such as Victor Hugo and facilitated by the efforts of various countries, was designed to create a unified system for the protection of authors' rights across international borders, thus addressing the rampant piracy that plagued artists and writers of the time. By the end of the 20th century, the Convention had been adopted by over 160 countries, solidifying its status as a cornerstone of intellectual property law worldwide.

The initial signing of the Berne Convention brought together representatives from 11 countries, who sought to establish a framework that would ensure creators were acknowledged and compensated for their works, regardless of where those works were published. The treaty set forth critical principles, such as the "automatic protection" of works and the requirement that signatory nations recognize and enforce the rights of foreign authors as if they were their own. Over the years, the Convention underwent several revisions, notably in Paris (1896), Berlin (1908), and Brussels (1948), adapting to the changing needs of the global literary and artistic landscape.
